newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thousands of poor Thais camp outside govt house.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of poor Thais camp outside govt house.

text.p: Armed with food and camping gear, thousands of poor northeastern Thais streamed into Bangkok on Saturday, rallied near Government House and declared they would not leave until their demands for social justice were met.
A well-organised group of about 3,000 people poured into the capital in buses, trucks and trains late on Friday and by noon on Saturday, the number had swelled to about 7,000, police said.

"We expect that at least 15,000 members of Assembly of the Poor will camp here," said Bamrung Kayota, political activist and secretary-general of the self-proclaimed Assembly of the Poor, which organised the protest.
The protesters from 10 provinces in the northeast demanded the government free them from their long-standing debts to the state-owned Bank of Agriculture and Cooperatives.
They also want the government to settle land disputes, offer compensation for building dams on land they claim and pay higher prices for their agricultural produce.
"The past two governments agreed to settle all these problems but none of them have acted on their promise," said Bamrung told Reuters.

"Now we have the government of Chavalit Yongchaiyudh who claims to be the prime minister of the poor people. He has to settle all these problem for us, otherwise the poor people will stay here until our demands are met."

The protesters who arrived in Bangkok on Saturday brought sacks of rice, dried fish, cooking utensils and camping gear. They began to erect shelters on two roads outside Government House as about 100 policeman watched silently.

"We will live here until the government agrees to provide a plot of land for each of us to do farming for a living," Wannee Chadeeduang, 71, from Unbol Rajatani, told Reuters as she prepared food for seven family members.
She said farm land near her house had been innundated with water, depriving her of a livelihood, after the government built a dam in in Ubon Ratchathani 17 years ago.

Thawan Srithai, 40, from Prachinburi province, who led 140 families to the protest, said his village had lost their farm land after border patrol police erected a camp in their area that encroached onto their land.
The Assembly of the Poor has launched a series of similar protests in recent years but their demands have never been met by governments in power.

On Monday, Chavalit went to the northeast for talks with Assembly representatives to try and stop them from marching into Bangkok. But protesters said he did not give dates for settling their problems and they had come to Bangkok to pressure him.
Interior Minister Sanh Thienthong told reporters that Chavalit had agreed to a demand that the government raise the price it pays farmers for tapioca.
"I dont know the real intention of their rally because we reached agreement on the price of tapioca last week," he said, accusing the organisers of rabble-rousing.
"I notice this same group of people every time there are protests. Maybe their occupation is organising mobs," he said.
However, he said the government would provide medical care and mobile toilets as long as the protesters stayed.
